DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (CNN) -- The United Arab Emirates has refused to grant a visa to a female Israeli tennis player, preventing her from competing in the Sony Ericsson World Tennis Association Tour in Dubai, the WTA said in a statement Sunday. The UAE has refused to grant a visa allowing Shahar Peer to compete in Dubai. Shahar Peer would have been the first Israeli athlete to participate in a professional sporting event in the UAE, CNN Sports correspondent Pedro Pinto said. The UAE has no diplomatic ties with Israel. Peer told CNN on Sunday evening she was "very, very disappointed" to be denied access to the tournament. "Any player that qualifies should attend, and I was prevented," she said from Israel. "I'm glad the WTA support me. A red line was crossed for every athlete in the world -- politics should be kept separate from sports." The governing body of women's tennis said it was "deeply disappointed" that Peer was being denied entry to the country hosting the tournament, but it did not cancel the competition, which began Sunday. The move runs counter to WTA policy, which says no player should be barred from competing in a tournament for which she has qualified. Dubai could lose its membership in the WTA tour next year over the ban on Peer, according to WTA rules. That would mean professional players could compete only in exhibition matches in Dubai, the results of which would not count in pro rankings. Government officials in Dubai have not responded to CNN's request to comment over their refusal to allow Peer to compete in the event. "Ms. Peer has earned the right to play in the tournament, and it is regrettable that the UAE is denying her this right," said Larry Scott, chairman and chief executive of the tour.  Watch Scott express disappointment » . "Following various consultations, the tour has decided to allow the tournament to continue to be played this week, pending further review by the tour's board of directors." The patron of the Dubai Tennis Championships is Dubai's ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Makhtoum. Two million dollars in prize money is on the line. Al-Makhtoum told CNN in 2004 that Dubai would accept Israeli students to a school dedicated to students from the Middle East who are talented at sports. In 2003, Dubai hosted World Bank and International Monetary Fund meetings, which Israeli government officials attended. The Israeli flag -- among other member states' flags -- is still part of a globe monument in Dubai. Peer, 21, is ranked 48th in the world among female tennis players. She was allowed to compete at the Doha tournament in Qatar last year, where she received a warm welcome, according to Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz. Qatar, another Gulf Arab state, froze diplomatic ties with Israel after Israel's military offensive in Gaza last month. Peer downplayed the political undertones of her participation in last year's Doha tournament, telling Haaretz that she didn't come to Qatar "to help the politics of course." But she added that if her playing in the tournament "can help for peace or anything, I'd be really happy." Scott said the tour will "review appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer" as well as "appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament." Peer was advised Saturday by tournament and WTA officials of the denial of her visa while she was participating in a tournament in Pattaya, Thailand, according to a WTA statement. The Dubai Tennis Championships runs through February 28.

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (CNN) — The United Arab Emirates has refused to grant a visa to Israeli tennis player Shahar Peer, preventing her from competing in the Sony Ericsson World Tennis Association Tour event in Dubai, the WTA said in a statement Sunday.

Peer would have been the first Israeli athlete to take part in a professional sporting event in the UAE, CNN Sports correspondent Pedro Pinto said. The UAE has no diplomatic ties with Israel.

Speaking to CNN from Israel on Sunday evening, Peer said she was “very, very disappointed” to be denied entry to the tournament.

“Any player that qualifies should attend, and I was prevented,” she said. “I’m glad the WTA support me. A red line was crossed for every athlete in the world — politics should be kept separate from sports.”

The governing body of women’s tennis said it was “deeply disappointed” that Peer had been denied entry to the country hosting the tournament. However, it did not cancel the competition, which began Sunday.

The decision runs counter to WTA policy, which states that no player should be barred from competing in a tournament for which she has qualified. Under WTA rules, Dubai could lose its membership in the WTA Tour next year over the ban on Peer. Such a move would mean professional players could compete in Dubai only in exhibition matches, the results of which would not count toward professional rankings.

Government officials in Dubai have not responded to CNN’s request for comment regarding their refusal to allow Peer to compete in the event.

“Ms. Peer has earned the right to play in the tournament, and it is regrettable that the UAE is denying her this right,” said Larry Scott, chairman and chief executive of the tour. “Following various consultations, the tour has decided to allow the tournament to continue to be played this week, pending further review by the tour’s board of directors.”

The patron of the Dubai Tennis Championships is Dubai’s ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Makhtoum. Two million dollars in prize money is at stake.

Al-Makhtoum told CNN in 2004 that Dubai would accept Israeli students at a school dedicated to athletically gifted students from the Middle East. In 2003, Dubai hosted meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, which Israeli government officials attended. The Israeli flag, along with those of other member states, remains part of a globe monument in Dubai.

Peer, 21, is ranked 48th in the world among female tennis players. She was permitted to compete last year at the tournament in Doha, Qatar, where she received a warm welcome, according to the Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz. Qatar, another Gulf Arab state, froze diplomatic ties with Israel after Israel’s military offensive in Gaza last month.

Peer downplayed the political undertones of her participation in last year’s Doha tournament, telling Haaretz that she had not come to Qatar “to help the politics of course.” However, she added that if her playing in the tournament “can help for peace or anything, I’d be really happy.”

Scott said the tour would “review appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer,” as well as “appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament.”

Peer was informed Saturday by tournament and WTA officials that her visa had been denied while she was competing in a tournament in Pattaya, Thailand, according to a WTA statement.

The Dubai Tennis Championships runs through February 28.

Scott said the WTA would examine “appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer” and consider “appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament.”

**Visa Denial for Israeli Tennis Player Shahar Pe’er Puts Politics at Center Court in Dubai**

*Dubai, United Arab Emirates* — The Dubai Tennis Championships, long promoted as one of the sport’s most cosmopolitan stops, has been thrust into an international controversy after Israeli player Shahar Pe’er was denied entry to the United Arab Emirates, turning a high-profile tennis tournament into the latest arena where Middle East politics and global sport collide.

Pe’er, one of Israel’s most prominent athletes and a regular competitor on the women’s tour, was scheduled to compete in the women’s event in Dubai. But organizers confirmed that she was unable to enter the country after UAE authorities refused to grant her a visa. The decision has drawn criticism from tennis officials, players, sponsors and commentators who say the move undermines the principle that sporting competition should be open to qualified athletes regardless of nationality.

The denial comes amid heightened regional tensions linked to Israel’s policies and conflict in the Palestinian territories, issues that have long shaped diplomatic relations between Israel and many Arab states. The UAE, like several countries in the region at the time, did not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, and Israeli passport holders often faced travel restrictions. Still, the decision to exclude a player from a major international sporting event has raised difficult questions for the Women’s Tennis Association and for global sports bodies more broadly: Can tournaments be staged in countries that do not guarantee access to all eligible competitors?

WTA officials responded sharply, signaling that the matter could have consequences for Dubai’s standing on the tour. The organization has emphasized that tournaments are expected to operate under rules of equal access and fair competition. While the WTA has expanded aggressively into new markets, including the Gulf, the Pe’er case has exposed the tension between commercial growth and the political realities of host nations.

The controversy also placed fellow players in a difficult position. Some expressed sympathy for Pe’er and concern about the precedent the decision could set. Others chose to compete while calling for tennis authorities to address the issue at an institutional level. The most visible rebuke came from prominent figures in the sport who argued that excluding a player because of nationality is incompatible with tennis’s international identity.

American star Venus Williams, who competed in the event, said publicly that she supported Pe’er’s right to play and described the situation as regrettable, while also stressing the importance of engagement and dialogue. Her comments reflected the balancing act many athletes face when political disputes intrude on competition: condemning discrimination without necessarily boycotting an event that is part of their professional calendar.

Sponsors and broadcasters were also drawn into the dispute. The Tennis Channel reportedly reconsidered its coverage, and corporate partners faced pressure to explain their association with a tournament where an eligible player had been barred. For global sport, commercial partnerships depend heavily on the image of inclusivity and fair play; cases like Pe’er’s threaten that image and force companies to weigh business interests against reputational risk.

The incident is not isolated. Sport has often served as both a bridge and a battleground in international politics. Apartheid-era South Africa was barred from many competitions for decades. Olympic boycotts during the Cold War turned athletic events into expressions of geopolitical alignment. More recently, athletes from countries in conflict have faced visa complications, security concerns or pressure to withdraw from matches against politically sensitive opponents.

Tennis, though individual in structure, is particularly vulnerable to these tensions because its tours are global and require athletes to cross borders almost weekly. A player’s nationality can become a diplomatic issue, especially when tournaments are held in countries with restrictive visa policies or strained relations with other states.

Pe’er herself has previously been a symbol of sport’s potential to cut through political barriers. As an Israeli athlete competing internationally, she has played opponents from countries whose governments have hostile or limited relations with Israel. Her participation in global tournaments has often been treated as routine within tennis circles, where rankings and qualification are supposed to determine entry. The Dubai decision disrupted that assumption.

Critics of the UAE’s decision argue that allowing politics to determine participation damages the credibility of international competition. If a host country can exclude one athlete because of nationality, they warn, other governments could do the same, fragmenting global sport along diplomatic lines.

Supporters of the UAE’s position, or those more sympathetic to it, point to the broader political climate in the region and public anger toward Israel. They argue that governments must consider domestic opinion and security concerns when granting entry. But tennis officials and human rights advocates counter that security arguments should be specific and evidence-based, not used as a blanket justification for barring athletes.

The fallout has intensified scrutiny of the WTA’s decision to award major events to countries where political restrictions may conflict with tour rules. Dubai has become one of the wealthiest and most prestigious non-Grand Slam stops, offering large prize money and attracting elite players. Its rise reflects the Gulf region’s broader investment in international sport, from tennis and golf to Formula One and football.

That investment has brought major events, global attention and commercial opportunity. But it has also raised recurring questions about “sportswashing” — the use of international sport to project openness and modernity while deflecting criticism of political restrictions, human rights concerns or regional policies. The Pe’er case gives those criticisms a concrete example, suggesting that the values marketed by global sport can clash with the policies of host states.

For the WTA, the immediate challenge is whether to punish Dubai, demand guarantees for future participation, or risk appearing to tolerate discrimination. Any response will be watched closely by other sports organizations navigating similar issues. A weak response could encourage future exclusions; a strong one could jeopardize lucrative relationships in a region increasingly central to the sports economy.

The men’s tour has also faced related questions. Israeli male players have encountered similar uncertainty when attempting to compete in Gulf events, prompting tennis authorities to seek assurances from organizers and governments. The issue is therefore unlikely to disappear with Pe’er’s absence from one tournament.

At its core, the dispute illustrates a recurring contradiction in international sport. Governing bodies often describe athletic competition as a neutral space, separate from politics. But tournaments depend on governments for visas, security, funding and infrastructure. When states control access, politics can determine who gets to play.

For Shahar Pe’er, the immediate consequence is straightforward: she lost the opportunity to compete in a major tournament for which she was otherwise eligible. For tennis, the consequences may be broader. The Dubai controversy has forced the sport to confront whether its commitment to open competition is absolute — or whether it bends when money, diplomacy and regional politics are involved.

As the tournament continues without her, the matches on court may decide rankings and prize money. But the larger contest is unfolding off the court, where tennis officials, governments, sponsors and players are being asked to define what international sport is supposed to stand for when politics refuses to stay outside the gates.
